articles.title: Iran regime under pressure as rebel groups escalate attacks in volatile southeast
articles.summary: A coalition of armed rebel groups is stepping up attacks against Iranian regime forces in the country's volatile southeast, raising questions about Tehran's...
articles.body:
A new coalition of Iranian opposition groups in the restive southeastern provinces of Sistan and Baluchistan and Kerman in the Islamic Republic have launched a string of armed attacks against the clerical regime in the region.

The six strikes claimed by the coalition known as the People's Fighters Front (JMM) have contributed to instability in the provinces, raising pressing questions about whether armed resistance against the clerical regime in Tehran will spread and if the regime can retain control over Sistan and Baluchistan, which is a majority Iranian Sunni province.

Iran is largely a Shiite Muslim country, and the minority Iranian Sunni population has faced discrimination over the decades. Sistan and Baluchistan is the second largest of the 31 Iranian provinces.

Mardo Soghom, an Iran expert who has written extensively about the Islamic Republic, told Fox News Digital, "The Sunni unrest can stretch the regime's military and internal security capabilities and have a psychological impact on its forces, in addition to what they experienced during the 40-day operation by the U.S. and Israel . The armed groups would not be able to establish control of the south-east, but they can seriously weaken the regime's control."

He added, "Whether these forces are receiving assistance from the Islamic Republic's adversaries — being that the Gulf Arab states or even Israel and the U.S. — remains an open question."

According to an October Human Rights Activist News Agency (HRANA) report , "The pace of violence accelerated significantly in recent weeks [in the provinces] with 18 incidents recorded in just the final 18 days of the reporting period, surpassing the total for any previous full month."

JMM coalesced as an opposition coalition in Dec. 2025 through an amalgam of Baloch nationalist organizations with the militant Sunni group Jaish al-Adl.

HRANA documented "at least 63 armed incidents were recorded across Iran's southeastern provinces of Sistan and Baluchistan and Kerman between March 31 and Oct.10, 2026, amid a sharp escalation in armed violence in the region."

The armed resistance resulted in "at least 94 people dead and 33 injured, while official sources reported 87 fatalities and 10 injuries."

The Baloch coalition stunned the regime on Oct. 14 with the assassinations of women members of the Basij paramilitaries, including a commander and a police officer in Sistan and Baluchistan Province. The Basij has been designated a terrorist entity by the U.S. government because it falls under the American-classified terrorist movement Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Just days before the attack on the female Basij commander, Iranian regime-controlled media reported that Nosrat Eftekhari, deputy for Cultural and Social Affairs of the Provincial Law Enforcement Command, was killed by a roadside bomb in Zahedan, Sistan and Baluchistan provinces.

Jason Brodsky, policy director at United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), told Fox News Digital that "There have been periodic cycles of unrest in Sistan and Baluchistan Province over the years. What we are now witnessing is an uptick in such activity. The current commander of the IRGC's Ground Forces, Mohammad Karami used to be governor of the province and commanded IRGC forces there. His experience in the province was one of the reasons Karami was elevated to the post in 2025 given the sensitive security situation in the country."

Brodsky continued that "I don't see any imminent threat in terms of such a seizure of control, but a red line for Iranians, especially in the opposition, is preserving the territorial integrity of Iran. That needs to be understood in Western capitals."

Khalilullah Balochi, who is a Baluch activist and journalist, told Iran International that "The activities of these groups are not new; what is new is the intensification of attacks."

JMM's devastating attacks targeting the brutal Iranian regime have generated attention from Iranian dissidents and experts.

Navid Mohebbi, who worked as a Persian media analyst for the State Department's Public Affairs Bureau, told Fox News Digital "The newly formed popular Fighters Front has carried out a series of relatively successful attacks against mid-level regime officials and security personnel in Sistan and Baluchistan province in recent months, drawing a degree of public attention. At a time when the regime is executing protesters on a daily basis, the killing of certain mid-ranking security and military operatives has been met with some satisfaction among segments of Iranian society."

He warned, however, that "Nevertheless, the Iranian public remains deeply cautious and largely distrustful of such groups. Two major concerns underpin this distrust: the possibility of separatist ambitions and the influence of radical Islamism, which is fundamentally at odds with the increasingly secular outlook of Iranian society."

Mohebbi sees encouraging signs from the JMM, including "the coalition's recent statements, unlike the rhetoric traditionally associated with similar groups, contain no explicit references to Baluch separatism. Instead, the coalition has identified its primary objective as dismantling the system of Velayat-e Faqih (Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist) and liberating the country from its oppression. It has explicitly declared that it seeks 'an Iran for all Iranians."'

He continued that "The reality is that these groups lack the capacity to confront the regime in conventional warfare . Through guerrilla operations, however, they can inflict significant psychological blows on the regime and its security establishment. Whether their activities can gain traction beyond Sistan and Baluchistan will depend largely on their ability to sustain what appears to be an effort to earn broader public trust."

Beni Sabti, an Iran expert at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) in Israel, told Fox News Digital the coalition has "a lot of guns" and created an "armed rebellion" against the Iranian regime in the provinces. He said, however, the armed upheaval is limited to the region Baluchistan.

Sabti, who was born in Tehran, said the clerical regime in the capital Tehran does not exercise solid control over the provinces, which resembles parts of South America where some governments lost sovereignty to militias.

He said that there are no reporters in the restive region. As a result, it is difficult to secure accurate news. Sabti said the "IRGC has a headquarters there to fight against these Baluchis." The JMM coalition "can only continue to harm the soldiers and, from time to time, kill a commander. There are a lot of these local commanders in Iran. It is not like an air force commander."

articles.title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says
articles.summary: From the shocking lack of PPE to restrictions on visitors - the key points from the sixth Covid inquiry report.
articles.body:
The sixth report of the Covid inquiry is highly critical of the way the government tried to protect people in care settings in the UK.

Around 500,000 people were living in care homes at the start of the pandemic – with another million receiving care in their own homes.

The inquiry said action to protect them came too late, causing devastating consequences.

There were more than 43,000 recorded deaths involving Covid in care homes between March 2020 and July 2022. Here are the key findings of the 287-page report.

At the start of the pandemic, the then-health secretary in England, Matt Hancock, said the UK government had placed "a protective ring" around care homes.

But the inquiry says this was not the case, listing a catalogue of failings.

It says the care sector appeared to be "something of an afterthought".

A lack of personal protective equipment (PPE) meant staff had to resort to makeshift workarounds, including bin bags, festival waterproof ponchos and painters' overalls.

The report is also critical of the way hospital patients who may be infected with Covid were moved to care homes to make space for others.

The decision was understandable given the need to free up beds for Covid patients.

But, without sufficient testing, it was important to keep these people separate and isolate them from others in case they were infected.

Official guidance in March 2020 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland did not request this. That, the report says, was a significant oversight.

Long-standing weaknesses undermined response

When the pandemic started, high levels of staff vacancies and turnover in the social care sector meant that the workforce was "fragile and lacking resilience".

This undermined the ability of the sector to respond to the pandemic, the inquiry says.

For example, care homes tend to rely heavily on agency staff who work in a variety of different homes. But a desire not to have staff going into multiple homes, to reduce the risk of infection transmission, meant staff shortages got even worse.

Financially, care providers struggled too, as the number of people using services dropped.

And for a sector that uses zero-hours contracts, there was a lack of financial support to help care staff stay off work if there was concern they might be infected.

The response also suffered because of the fragmented nature of the system, with thousands of different providers and services overseen by councils. It meant the sector was more distant from government than the NHS.

The pandemic, the inquiry said, exposed and exacerbated these existing weaknesses.

Visiting restrictions were too tough – and caused harm

The report is clear that precautionary steps taken to restrict visiting, as part of infection control, went too far.

It acknowledges there was little choice to introduce bans on visitors at the start of the pandemic, saying that was rational.

But as the pandemic progressed, so did the balance between the benefits and harms of restrictions.

Visits are extremely important, allowing loved ones to help residents with everything from personal care to maintaining their mental health.

By September 2020, evidence suggested visitors posed a "marginal risk" – staff were judged to be the key entry point for infections.

The four UK nations then started to relax their guidance, but many care homes failed to implement this and visiting remained heavily restricted.

This, says the inquiry, resulted in a significant decline in the health and wellbeing of residents.

Concern over blanket do not resuscitate orders

CPR (Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation), including chest compressions, can be life-saving if a person's heart has stopped beating.

But doctors can sometimes opt not to resuscitate people - as can individuals themselves in advance - for example, if the individual is extremely frail or has a life-limiting illness.

This should be done on an individual basis and the use of blanket do not resuscitate orders (DNACPR) is considered unlawful.

The inquiry says it heard evidence of GPs imposing blanket DNACPRs on care home residents.

And it pointed to records showing a sharp increase in orders being put in place – they jumped from 16,800 to 26,500 in the first nine months of the pandemic.

This concern mirrors an earlier Care Quality Commission investigation which found evidence of unacceptable and inappropriate DNACPRs being put in place.

The impact on staff working in care homes was huge, affecting their mental health and wellbeing, the inquiry said.

Some moved into the care homes where they worked, in an attempt to protect residents from infection. One care home owner in Wales described how 39 staff moved in for a fortnight at the start of the pandemic.

Seeing so many residents die placed an enormous strain on workers, who often had to provide end-of-life care to multiple people at the same time.

One care home, for example, lost half of its residents over the course of three weeks.

Staff told the inquiry of the deep distress they suffered.

"Staff were sitting on video calls with families, saying their last goodbye to loved ones. That was horrendous… staff were crying with the residents, because it was just so emotional for them," one said.

articles.title: In 2020, a Georgia woman transferred her interest in a home to her stepson despite concerns about her memory; a jury later rescinded the deed and awarded $57,600 in damages, and an October 19 appeals court upheld the verdict
articles.summary: A family home became the centre of a fraud dispute after a Georgia woman transferred her property interest to her stepson while reportedly experiencing
articles.body: A family home became the centre of a fraud dispute after a Georgia woman transferred her property interest to her stepson while reportedly experiencing memory loss. Years later, the courts were asked to determine whether the transfer could stand and whether the jury’s decision should be overturned. On October 19, 2026, the Georgia Court of Appeals upheld the verdict against the stepson, leaving in place the cancellation of the deed and a total award of $57,600 in damages. According to the court’s opinion, published by Justia in James Heard v. Rany L. Logan, the appeal focused on objections concerning the jury’s oath and alleged juror misconduct, rather than a fresh determination of the original property dispute.How the dispute over the Georgia home beganThe case concerned Lynette Murphy, whose stepson, James Heard, received her interest in a home in Rome, Georgia, in 2020. According to the court record, Murphy had reportedly been experiencing memory loss since 2013. Her guardian and conservator, Rany Logan, subsequently alleged that Heard persuaded her to transfer her property interest despite her lack of capacity to make that decision.Logan filed a verified complaint against Heard in 2021, claiming that Heard had refused demands to return the property. The lawsuit included claims involving rescission of the deed, exploitation of a disabled adult, exploitation of an elderly person, fraud and deceit. Logan sought legal remedies intended to reverse the transfer and protect Murphy’s interests. The claims also sought a constructive trust, an injunction, punitive damages and attorney fees.The dispute eventually proceeded to trial, where a jury ruled in Logan’s favour. It ordered the deed rescinded and awarded $27,600 in damages for fraud, along with $30,000 in punitive damages. Together, the two awards amounted to $57,600.Why the stepson challenged the verdictHeard asked the trial court to overturn the verdict or order a new trial. His challenge rested on two principal arguments. First, he contended that the jury panel had not been administered the oath required under Georgia law. He argued that this procedural failure invalidated the verdict. Second, Heard claimed that juror misconduct had compromised the proceedings. The concern arose after a juror reportedly searched for information about Logan online and told fellow jurors that Logan had previously tried to take other people’s property.Heard argued that the incident warranted a mistrial. The trial court rejected his request, prompting him to appeal to the Georgia Court of Appeals.What the appeals court decidedIn its October 19 ruling, the appellate court rejected both arguments and affirmed the lower court’s judgment. On the jury oath issue, the court acknowledged that the prescribed oath had not been administered. However, it explained that, in a civil case, the failure to administer the oath could be waived if a party did not object at the appropriate time. The court noted that Heard had been present and represented throughout the proceedings but had not raised the issue before the trial court. It also observed that the jury had received instructions about considering the evidence, assessing witnesses and following the law.Although the omission was an error, the judges concluded that Heard had not demonstrated that it undermined the fairness or integrity of the trial. The court therefore found no basis to invalidate the verdict. The judges also rejected the argument concerning juror misconduct. According to the opinion, the trial judge removed the juror who had conducted the online search and replaced him with an alternate who had not heard the improper comment.The judge then questioned the remaining jurors individually about what they had heard and whether they could decide the case impartially, relying only on the evidence presented at trial. Each indicated that they could remain fair. The appeals court found no abuse of discretion in the trial judge’s decision to deny a mistrial.What the ruling means for the property disputeThe October 19 decision leaves the jury’s original judgment intact. The deed remains rescinded, and the $57,600 award stands, comprising $27,600 in fraud damages and $30,000 in punitive damages. The ruling also illustrates the importance of raising procedural objections at the appropriate stage of a civil trial. Even when a court identifies an error, that does not automatically mean the verdict must be overturned. Appellate judges consider the applicable legal standards, the circumstances of the proceedings and whether the alleged error provides grounds for reversal.In this case, the court concluded that neither the jury oath issue nor the handling of the juror’s online search justified a new trial. Its decision affirmed the judgment in Logan’s favour in the dispute involving Murphy’s home.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 1979, Keith Haring painted a mural directly on a New York loft's walls and ceiling before it vanished behind drywall; its owner later restored the 8,000-square-foot home, now listed for $25 million
articles.summary: Somewhere behind the walls of a New York loft, an artwork by Keith Haring spent decades out of sight, protected by an unlikely layer of drywall.
articles.body: Somewhere behind the walls of a New York loft, an artwork by Keith Haring spent decades out of sight, protected by an unlikely layer of drywall. Painted long before the artist became an international name, the mural survived a change of occupants, a restaurant conversion and years of concealment. Today, it is the centrepiece of an extraordinary Tribeca property: an 8,000-square-foot triplex listed for $25 million, claims an online report by art website Artsy.A mural painted into the buildingAccording to Artsy, located at 260 West Broadway in the landmarked American Thread Building, the loft carries a piece of New York art history that cannot simply be taken down and moved elsewhere. Haring created the monochrome mural in 1979, while studying at the School of Visual Arts (SVA), which then operated a student gallery on the building’s lower floor.Working with shoe polish and alcohol rather than conventional art materials, Haring painted directly onto an iron column, a structural beam and the ceiling, states the report. The resulting composition features interlocking forms and energetic black lines characteristic of the visual language that would later make him one of the most recognisable figures in contemporary art.When SVA vacated the premises in the early 1980s and the space became a restaurant, wallboard was installed over the artwork, adds the online report.Rediscovered after decadesThe artwork resurfaced in 2007, when the building’s previous owners uncovered it largely intact. Its survival was remarkable, given the unconventional materials used and the fact that it had remained hidden for decades.The mural is unsigned, but its authenticity has since been confirmed by the Keith Haring Foundation, states the report too. Its discovery also offered a glimpse of the artist’s early years, when he was still a young student working outside the conventional gallery system.Adam Zoia, chief executive of Glocap Tech and the loft’s current owner, recognised the distinctive style when he encountered the mural. He purchased the property in 2021 and embarked on a two-year renovation, reworking the expansive interiors while keeping the artwork at the heart of the design, explains the report by Artsy.Living around a piece of art historyThe renovation was shaped by the practical challenge of protecting a work that forms part of the building itself. A bar was installed in front of the mural, creating a buffer against accidental contact and spills while allowing it to remain visible.The arrangement reflects an unusual reality for whoever buys the property: the artwork is inseparable from the architecture. It cannot be removed without fundamentally altering the structure on which Haring painted it.As per the report, that connection also complicates its valuation. Art dealer Jenn Singer has pointed to the mural’s site-specific nature as a defining factor, placing it in a different category from works that can be sold and displayed independently.A $25 million home with a unique legacyFor the next owner, the purchase will involve more than acquiring a sizeable Manhattan residence. The triplex comes with the responsibility of preserving an original work by an artist whose influence on contemporary visual culture remains considerable.The mural’s value is difficult to separate from the loft around it, and its significance extends beyond the price attached to the listing. Created by a young Haring decades before his rise to international fame, it has endured by chance, hidden in plain sight. Now, as the Tribeca property enters the market for $25 million, its most compelling feature is not simply its scale or address. It is a piece of art history that has become part of the home itself.Image Courtesy: Wikipedia and Keith Haring Foundation. articles.title: Dumfries and Galloway gets global travel destination recognition
articles.summary: The travel experts praise the hiking, cycling and stargazing opportunities in Dumfries and Galloway.
articles.body:
A "thrilling and overlooked" part of Scotland has received recognition as one of the best travel destinations on the planet

Dumfries and Galloway is the only UK site on the National Geographic's Best of the World list for 2027.

It praises the area's attractions including its role as a dark sky destination for stargazers, as well as its cycling and walking routes.

Tourism body the South of Scotland Destination Alliance (SSDA) said it was an "extraordinary opportunity" to promote the region to "new audiences around the world".

National Geographic releases its Best of the World list every year. It celebrates places and travel experiences that "illuminate the world and the diversity of communities and people within it".

Selected by editors from around the world in collaboration with experts and expedition leaders, the list features both up-and-coming destinations and established locations with "something new to offer".

Last year's list included the Dolomites mountain range in Italy as well as Beijing and Rio de Janeiro.

New Scottish Dark Sky Observatory plans get the green light

The medieval monk's journey that became a global travel 'essential'

National Geographic describes Dumfries and Galloway as "one of Scotland's most thrilling and overlooked destinations" offering "landscapes as wild as the Highlands and as romantic as the Islands".

It praised the Scottish Dark Sky Observatory, currently under construction in the Galloway Forest Park, as "one of the world's best spots for celestial viewing".

Other highlighted attractions include a new coastal hiking trail around the Rhins of Galloway and the region's world-class biking terrain, which it describes as being "spruced up just in time to host the opening leg of the 2027 Tour de France."

The latest recognition highlights the region's reputation as a dark sky destination.

In 2009, the Galloway Forest Park was designated as the UK's first international dark sky park and a new observatory is due to open next year at Clatteringshaws.

It also recognises the area's coasts and castles, food and drink and unique wildlife and comes after a south of Scotland walking route was recognised in the Lonely Planet Best in Travel Guide.

St Cuthbert's Way, which follows the journey of a medieval monk through the Borders and Northumberland was chosen as one of the world's top travel experiences.

Matthew Wallace Jnr runs the Cairndale Hotel and Spa in Dumfries, winner of best hotel at the South of Scotland Thistle Awards earlier this month.

"There's a growing sense of energy, ambition and pride across the south of Scotland, with businesses coming together under the Scotland Starts Here brand to show the world what we offer," he said.

"Having a global name like National Geographic shine a light on Dumfries and Galloway is another exciting sign of that momentum."

At the western edge of the region, Central Cafe owner Romano Petrucci is chairman of the Stranraer Development Trust and the town's oyster festival.

"It's exciting to see National Geographic recognising what Dumfries and Galloway has to offer international visitors, and here in Stranraer we want to make the most of that attention," he said.

"With the oyster festival and growing enthusiasm for the vision of a major visitor attraction on the East Pier, there's a real sense of pride and possibility in the town.

"For businesses like mine, success means more people stopping, enjoying a meal, exploring our shops and discovering a place they'll want to come back to."

SSDA chief executive David Hope-Jones said the "wonderful recognition" reflected the "energy, creativity and hard work of tourism businesses and communities across the region".

"National Geographic's recognition gives us an extraordinary opportunity to introduce Dumfries and Galloway to new audiences around the world."

The recognition was welcomed by the local council, as well as Visit Scotland chief executive Vicki Miller, who described it as a "testament to the region's strong pull for visitors".

"Tourism and events are hugely important to the region, with the benefits of the visitor economy felt right across Dumfries and Galloway," she said.

"This exciting accolade will strengthen its reputation and profile as a first-class visitor destination."

articles.title: 'Nobody told me..that's very confusing': Indian man Kamlesh Shah charged with election fraud in US says he didn't know he was not supposed to vote
articles.summary: 67-year-old Kamlesh Navnitlal Shah, a retired dentist from California, said he had no idea that he was not supposed to vote in the 2024 election, as he
articles.body: 67-year-old Kamlesh Navnitlal Shah, a retired dentist from California, said he had no idea that he was not supposed to vote in the 2024 election, as he was a permanent resident but not a citizen. He has now been charged with fraudulently registering to vote in US elections. After his name came up in the list of foreign nationals who voted in the election in California, he said he was scared as he was not aware of the situation. Dr Shah said he met an accident five to six years ago and was in a coma for six months, and can hardly talk or walk.Apart from Shah, another Indian on the list is 30-year-old Amandeep Kaur, a resident of Rancho Palos Verdes. According to the law enforcement record, Kaur is seeking to become a US citizen, and fraudulently registered to vote in December 2022 and then voted in the November 2024 US election.Shah said he went to the community center "to vote with my blind roommate". He said his was asked to produce his ID. "I showed them the ID and my Social Security card. They did something...I don't remember...it was a long time ago. They gave me the paperwork to vote. I thought I was registering to vote. I didn't know about my pending citizenship. I thought I must be a citizen. I had no idea I wasn't," Shah said, adding that nobody told him that he was not a citizen and was not supposed to vote.What is 'Operation Protect the Vote'?The administration said Operation Protect the Vote is a coordinated effort among all four California-based US Attorney's offices to combat and root out fraud in US elections. 11 foreign nationals among 28 total charged were arrested for voter fraud. All these 28 foreign nationals have Green cards but they are not US citizens and no one except US citizens are allowed to vote in US elections.The criminal charges include making false statements in a naturalization application and some of the defendants also are charged with fraudulent voter registration. Both charges are felonies that carry a maximum penalty of five years in federal prison.On October 13, the federal government provided a list of these individuals to California to ensure that their vote-by-mail ballots were set aside until these individuals’ citizenship status could be confirmed. California declined to assist the federal government in setting aside their ballots, prompting a lawsuit by the United States that seeks a court order to prevent the unlawful dilution of American citizens’ votes and to uphold the integrity of our elections.“Every illegal vote cancels out the vote of a lawful American citizen,” said Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter. “Each of the 28 defendants charged today appears on the list of more than 20,000 likely noncitizen registrants we provided to California election officials last week. California refused to look at that list. Today's charges show exactly what that refusal puts at risk. California must verify the citizenship of those more than 20,000 registrants before mail-in ballots are counted.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Burqa-clad, e-rickshaw clue: How a change of transport helped police trace Shraddha Dubey to 11th-floor flat in Nagpur
articles.summary: NAGPUR: An e-rickshaw clue helped Nagpur police to track down burqa-clad Shraddha Dubey, prime accused in the sensational murder of Lucknow cafe owner,
articles.body: NAGPUR: An e-rickshaw clue helped Nagpur police to track down burqa-clad Shraddha Dubey, prime accused in the sensational murder of Lucknow cafe owner, Shiva Sharma, in Chinchbhuvan in Nagpur outskirts on Sunday.Shraddha was on the run for 10 days. Shraddha, her sister Rashmi Dubey and driver Tanveer Ali, alias Danish, were traced to a rented flat on the 11th floor of an apartment in Chinchbhuvan.A 24-hour surveillance operation, backed by CCTV footage, extraction of internet records, social media tracking and local intelligence, helped police nab the trio.The operation began after Uttar Pradesh Police contacted Nagpur commissioner of police Vishwas Nangare Patil for assistance in tracing the suspects after realizing the trio was fleeing towards central India.The top cop assigned the task to Crime Branch DCP Deepak Agarwal, who formed three teams under senior police inspectors Shubhangi Deshmukh and Nitin Chulpar. The teams worked on different leads to establish the suspects' movements across the city.As per police sources, the trio arrived in Nagpur in a rented vehicle bearing a Uttar Pradesh registration number. They reached Ganeshpeth and took an e-rickshaw to Chinchbhuvan.This change of transport proved crucial.Nagpur police examined footage from around 200 CCTV cameras to follow the e-rickshaw's route and identify the rented apartment, where the suspects were hiding.The crime branch team zeroed in on the flat and kept it under surveillance till Uttar Pradesh Special Task Force (STF) personnel arrived.A joint team then moved in and took the three into custody. They are expected to be produced in court for transit remand before being taken to Lucknow on WednesdayShraddha remained underground for 10 days, moving between Nepal, Agra, Lucknow and Kanpur before reaching Nagpur.The investigators suspect she used different communication methods to evade police surveillance. She was also allegedly wearing a burqa to conceal her identity while travelling with her sister and driver.The case concerns the death of 27-year-old Shiva Sharma, a Lucknow businessman who owned a cafe and restaurants. He died on October 9 after falling off the fourth floor of Awadh Green Apartments in the Hazratganj area.Shiva's mother, Ranjana, had accused Shraddha and her associates of murdering him, alleging he faced harassment, threats and physical assault.Lucknow police registered a murder case and launched a search for the accused. Shraddha later released a video claiming she was innocent and Sharma had died by suicide.Police are investigating the circumstances surrounding his death. articles.title: Air India Express flight suffers bird strike, lands safely in Bengaluru
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: An Air India Express flight from Bhogapuram in Andhra Pradesh to Bengaluru suffered a bird strike but landed safely at Kempegowda International
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An Air India Express flight from Bhogapuram in Andhra Pradesh to Bengaluru suffered a bird strike but landed safely at Kempegowda International Airport, with all 148 passengers and crew members unharmed on Tuesday.The incident occurred on Monday, following which the aircraft was inspected by technical teams to assess any damage to its structure and engines. Such inspections are part of standard safety procedures after a bird strike to determine whether an aircraft can continue operating safely.An Air India Express spokesperson said the aircraft had been declared serviceable after the inspection and that there was no disruption to flight operations."Our Bhogapuram-Bengaluru flight reported a bird strike. The aircraft was inspected and has been declared serviceable. There has been no impact on our operations," the spokesperson said in a statement, as quoted by ANI.A similar incident was reported on October 17, when an Emirates flight from Dubai to Delhi suffered a bird strike while arriving in the national capital. The incident damaged the aircraft's nose cone and delayed its return flight to Dubai by more than 14 hours as repairs were required, according to reports.Bird strikes occur when birds collide with aircraft, potentially damaging components such as the nose, windscreen or engines. While many such incidents cause little or no damage, they can require technical inspections and repairs before an aircraft is cleared for its next flight.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Names on Saudi prison list, death sentences missing: Bangladesh furious over executions of two citizens
articles.summary: Bangladesh has expressed anger and sought a detailed explanation from Saudi Arabia after two of its citizens, Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akhter, were
articles.body: Bangladesh has expressed anger and sought a detailed explanation from Saudi Arabia after two of its citizens, Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akhter, were executed in Mecca on October 14 without prior notification to Dhaka. The government has questioned why their death sentences were missing from a list of convicted nationals sent by Saudi authorities on September 30, saying timely information could have allowed its diplomatic mission to explore possible intervention.As per reports by Bangladeshi outlet Prothom Alo, Dhaka is seeking copies of the verdicts, details of the judicial proceedings and confirmation of whether the two were allowed to defend themselves. The executions have raised concerns over a possible lapse in consular communication between the two countries.Bangladesh questions Saudi Arabia over missing sentencesOn Monday, Bangladesh's consul general in Jeddah, Md Sakhawat Hossain, raised the issue with Farid bin Saad Al Shehri, director general of Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Bangladesh also sent another diplomatic note seeking detailed information about the cases.According to officials at Bangladesh's ministry of foreign affairs, the Saudi official was unable to provide a satisfactory explanation for why the sentences had not been disclosed in the list supplied to Dhaka.The list, sent on September 30, included the names of Nazrul and Sweety, along with details of the offences they were accused of committing. However, it did not specify their sentences.According to Prothom Alo, a senior Bangladeshi official said that the latest diplomatic note sought detailed accounts of the cases, the steps taken during the judicial proceedings and whether the two had been given an opportunity to defend themselves.Bangladesh's Consul General confirmed that the meeting had taken place and another diplomatic note had been sent. He declined to disclose details of the discussions.The development follows earlier diplomatic exchanges over the executions. On October 15, the Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah sent a note to Saudi Arabia seeking information. On October 18, Dhaka raised the matter with Saudi Ambassador Abdullah Zafer bin Abiyah.'Very disappointing', says BangladeshState minister for foreign affairs Humaiun Kobir on Monday described the executions as “very disappointing” and said Bangladesh had sought an explanation from its Saudi counterpart over the apparent gap in information-sharing.“Bangladesh has a good and deep relationship with Saudi Arabia, particularly at the level of our Prime Minister. Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia are both signatories to the Geneva Conventions. There was a gap in information-sharing in this incident. We have sought an explanation from Saudi Arabia to find out why this gap occurred,” Kobir said.He said Bangladesh expected other countries to inform it when its citizens were detained or faced criminal proceedings, allowing its diplomatic missions to provide consular assistance.Kobir added that Bangladesh would similarly inform Saudi Arabia if a Saudi national were arrested in the country.State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said the government was still awaiting copies of the verdicts to understand the cases and determine what further steps could be taken.“Please wait until we know what the verdict says. After that, we will discuss the matter with the Saudi authorities and explore what can be done,” she said.She added that Bangladesh had not received detailed information about the individuals and was awaiting a formal response from Saudi Arabia.What Saudi Arabia says about the executionsAccording to the Saudi Press Agency, the country's Ministry of Interior said the two Bangladeshis were convicted of committing what it described as immoral acts inside a mosque in Mecca.The ministry said the pair were arrested and investigated before being referred to a competent court. They were sentenced to death under ta'zir, a category of punishment under Islamic law left to judicial discretion.Saudi authorities said the sentences were imposed because of the seriousness of the offence, the violation of the mosque's sanctity and the circumstances in which the acts were committed.The verdicts were upheld by the relevant judicial authority, and a royal order authorised their implementation. The executions were carried out separately in the Mecca region on October 14.During Monday's meeting in Jeddah, the Saudi side reportedly told Bangladeshi officials that the two had been sentenced by a lower court and that an appellate panel comprising 13 judges had upheld the verdicts.However, the list supplied to Bangladesh did not mention the sentences. The Saudi official was unable to provide a satisfactory answer when asked why this information had been omitted if the cases had followed due judicial process.Nazrul Islam's family seeks his bodyThe diplomatic dispute has also drawn attention to the plight of Nazrul Islam's family in Bangladesh. His parents say they were not informed in advance of his execution and learnt of his death through a telephone call from Saudi Arabia on October 14.Nazrul, who was from Brahmanbaria district, travelled to Saudi Arabia in November 2022 in the hope of improving his family's financial circumstances. He worked as a cleaner in the kingdom.His father, Abdul Basir, borrowed around Tk 6 lakh from relatives to send his eldest son abroad. Nazrul sent home about Tk 1.5 lakh during his first seven to eight months in Saudi Arabia, according to the family.Saudi authorities detained him on August 1, 2023. He remained in custody until his execution, more than three years later.The family said their last telephone conversation with Nazrul took place on October 11 and lasted around two minutes. They received no advance notice that his death sentence was about to be carried out.“The creditors are now pressuring me to repay the debt. I want my son’s body brought back home. If he was executed without just cause, I want justice,” Basir said.Nazrul's mother, Rahima Begum, has also appealed for his body to be returned so the family can see him one last time. Relatives said his paternal aunt, Abeda Begum, collapsed after hearing of his death and died later that night.The family has urged the Bangladeshi government to investigate the circumstances of the execution and arrange for the repatriation of his body at state expense.Questions over charges and legal assistanceThe information provided by Saudi Arabia to Bangladesh has raised further questions about the cases.The September 30 list reportedly identified Nazrul as having been convicted of cybercrime or an offence related to information technology. Sweety's entry mentioned adultery. Neither entry specified the sentence imposed.This differed from the Saudi Interior Ministry's public account, which described the offence as an immoral act inside a mosque.Bangladeshi officials have sought detailed records to clarify the charges, the judicial proceedings and the opportunity available to the defendants to defend themselves. The government has also questioned why its diplomatic mission was not informed of the death sentences in time to consider possible intervention.The precise circumstances of the cases and the legal assistance provided to the two defendants remain unclear from the information available to Bangladesh.Dhaka awaits response and considers repatriationBangladesh has said it will consider further steps after receiving the verdicts and a detailed response from Saudi Arabia. Shama Obaed said the government would explore the repatriation of the bodies once the requested information was received.Brahmanbaria deputy commissioner Md Abu Sayeed said the district administration would act in accordance with government instructions and applicable rules. He added that it had not received an application from Nazrul's family or specific instructions on the matter.Despite its concerns, Dhaka has stressed the importance of maintaining its close relationship with Riyadh. Kobir said discussions were under way to establish why the communication gap occurred.The central question for Bangladesh remains why the names of two citizens appeared on an official list of convicted nationals, while the death sentences that led to their executions were not disclosed.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Florida couple missed 66 mortgage payments on their Naples property; the husband later agreed to deposit $5,000 monthly during an appeal, but an October 19 federal ruling rejected his lawsuit against the bank
articles.summary: A Florida couple who missed 66 monthly mortgage payments on their Naples property have been involved in a legal dispute with their bank for nearly 17
articles.body: A Florida couple who missed 66 monthly mortgage payments on their Naples property have been involved in a legal dispute with their bank for nearly 17 years. During the dispute, the husband, Gregory Brian Myers, agreed to deposit $5,000 every month while he and his wife challenged the bank's attempt to take possession of the property. Years later, Myers accused the bank of breaking that agreement. However, on Monday a US federal appeals court rejected his challenge and upheld an earlier decision dismissing his lawsuit.According to the court records available on Justia, the dispute began in 2009, when US Bank took legal action against Myers and his wife, Barbara Ann Kelly, over unpaid mortgage instalments. A Florida court eventually ruled in the bank's favour after finding that the couple had failed to make 66 monthly payments. Both Myers and Kelly challenged that decision.The property had originally been purchased by Kelly, who took out a mortgage to pay for it. She later added Myers as a joint owner. US Bank National Association, acting on behalf of a mortgage-backed securities trust, held the mortgage on the property.Why Myers agreed to deposit $5,000 every monthAfter the Florida court allowed the bank to proceed with foreclosure, Myers and Kelly appealed the decision. Foreclosure is the legal process through which a lender can take and sell a property when mortgage payments are not made.While their appeals were pending, Myers filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in Maryland. This temporarily stopped the bank from moving ahead with certain actions to recover the property.US Bank then asked the bankruptcy court for permission to continue the foreclosure proceedings. The bank wanted to proceed with the couple's appeals and sell the property if the earlier judgment was upheld.In November 2016, Myers and the bank reached an agreement. The appeals could continue, but the bank could not sell the property until both had been finally decided in its favour.As part of the arrangement, Myers had to deposit $5,000 every month into a court account in Maryland. He later claimed that he had deposited a total of $70,000.The agreement also explained what would happen to that money. If the bank won the appeals, it could receive the deposited amount. However, the bank would have to count that money towards the debt owed by Myers or Kelly.In 2018, a Florida appeals court ruled against the couple and upheld the earlier foreclosure decision. This meant that the appeals which had prevented the bank from selling the property were over.Why the husband sued the bank againDespite the 2018 ruling, the dispute did not end. In 2024, Myers filed another lawsuit after the bank attempted to schedule a sale of the Naples property.He claimed that the bank's actions went against the agreement reached in 2016. He also accused the defendants of fraud and alleged that his constitutional rights had been violated.However, the federal district court found that his initial complaint did not clearly explain which of the people or organisations he had sued were responsible for the alleged wrongdoing. The court allowed him to revise his complaint.Myers then filed a new version, naming several differently identified US Bank entities and Credit Suisse First Boston Mortgage Acceptance Corp. This time, his allegations included breach of contract, constructive fraud and violations of a federal law governing debt collection practices.The court rejected his claims. One important reason was that the 2016 agreement had never promised to stop the bank from selling the property permanently.Instead, it had only prevented a sale while the couple's appeals were pending. Since those appeals had ended in 2018, the court found that the bank's later attempt to proceed with foreclosure did not break the agreement. The court also found that Myers had not provided enough facts to support his fraud allegation.What the October 19 court ruling saidMyers challenged the dismissal of his lawsuit, arguing that the lower court had not properly considered his claims. He also believed he should have been given another opportunity to correct his complaint.But the US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit did not agree. The judges found that Myers had failed to explain clearly how the bank had broken its agreement with him.Myers also argued that a separate bankruptcy filing in Washington, DC, should have prevented the court from deciding his case. The judges rejected this argument because he had filed the lawsuit himself. Bankruptcy protection against legal proceedings generally applies to cases brought against someone who has filed for bankruptcy.Another disagreement concerned the different names under which Myers had identified US Bank in his complaint. The appeals court found no reason to believe that treating them as one defendant had affected the outcome.The judges upheld the earlier decision to dismiss the lawsuit with prejudice, meaning Myers could not bring the same claims again in that case. They also rejected his request to have the judgment reconsidered.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Indian-origin couple sentenced in UK for Covid PPE fraud; millions spent on luxuries
articles.summary: An Indian-origin businessman has been sentenced to eight years in prison in the UK for defrauding companies through fake personal protective equipment
articles.body: An Indian-origin businessman has been sentenced to eight years in prison in the UK for defrauding companies through fake personal protective equipment (PPE) supply deals during the Covid-19 pandemic and using the money to fund a lavish lifestyle, including luxury cars, expensive watches and home renovations.Jogesh Bhandari, 59, from Loughborough, was sentenced at Leicester Crown Court on October 16 after failing to attend two earlier sentencing hearings, citing health issues. A judge subsequently ordered his arrest, according to Britain's National Crime Agency (NCA).Meanwhile, his wife, Meenakshi (Meena) Bhandari, and business associate Craig Morris, 43, were sentenced on October 7. Meena received a two-year prison sentence, suspended for two years, along with 250 hours of unpaid community work, while Morris was jailed for three years and nine months.The three were convicted of fraud and money laundering offences following a five-week trial in July.Investigators found that Bhandari and Morris had set up a company in 2020 to trade nitrile gloves, which were in high demand during the pandemic. They worked with Frank Labruzzo, a US Assistant Attorney General at the Louisiana State Department of Justice, who provided a fraudulent escrow service.The scheme involved securing large PPE contracts and diverting payments before the promised supplies were delivered.In November 2020, Bhandari agreed to supply 12 million boxes of gloves, but the money deposited into an escrow account was instead transferred to him, Labruzzo and other companies.The following month, he received another $2.7 million, withdrawing $500,000 almost immediately to settle debts belonging to him and his wife.In early 2021, Bhandari received more than $3.18 million for gloves intended for US hospitals, but the supplies never arrived. Another deal brought in $1.35 million, which was deposited directly into a business account controlled by Meena.Rather than fulfilling the contracts, the couple spent substantial amounts on personal expenses. According to the NCA, £126,000 went towards a new Porsche, while £200,000 was transferred to Morris.Bank records also revealed purchases of Rolex watches, jewellery and several vehicles, including an Audi A5, a Land Rover Discovery and a Volkswagen Golf. The couple also used the funds for home improvements, overseas holidays and repaying personal debts.The NCA investigation uncovered more than 47,000 messages exchanged between Bhandari and Morris, revealing how they coordinated their fraudulent activities.In one exchange, Bhandari wrote, "I need you to help me out with a scam…you need to pose as a previous satisfied customer". Morris responded, "I’ll do what I can to help."Paul Boniface, operations manager at the NCA, said the defendants had exploited legitimate businesses at a time when healthcare facilities were struggling to obtain essential protective equipment."While Bhandari was picking up his brand new luxury car and talking about how he couldn’t stop smiling, healthcare facilities had not received the vital PPE they needed at a time when demand was exponential and companies were millions of dollars out of pocket," he said.The agency said the fraud had consequences beyond the financial losses suffered by businesses, as the promised equipment failed to reach healthcare providers during the pandemic.You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi invoked the ideals of 'Ram Rajya' and called for public welfare, social justice and self-reliance while addressing
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi invoked the ideals of 'Ram Rajya' and called for public welfare, social justice and self-reliance while addressing Dussehra on Tuesday.Addressing the celebrations at the DDA Utsav Ground in IP Extension, East Delhi and participating in the traditional Ravan Dahan ceremony, PM Modi said the purpose of power was to serve people, not rule them, and stressed that the welfare of the poor and deprived sections must remain a priority.The Prime Minister also spoke about Lord Ram's ideals, the need to find solutions using India's own resources and the goal of building a developed and self-reliant nation. He said Vijayadashami symbolised the victory of good over evil.Here are the top quotes from PM Modi's address at the Dussehra celebrations:Ramrajya signifies a system of governance free from discrimination—a realm where justice prevails, and everyone is afforded equal opportunities.In such a system, the purpose of authority is not merely to rule, but to ensure the welfare of the people...Serving the poor and the marginalised must remain our highest priority.This country, its culture, and its ancestors have worshipped Lord Shri Ram for thousands of years. This faith is not only because Shri Ram defeated the demon king Ravana. This faith is also because Lord Ram gave us such ideals which are incomparable in the history of humanity. Lord Shri Ram faced so many difficulties in his life, but he never left the path of truth and policy.The life of Lord Ram offers us a profound lesson: no matter how great the crisis or how daunting the challenge, we must not rely on others. We must recognise our own potential, trust in our own resources, transform our resolve into strength, and forge solutions through our own hard work.Today, we too must move forward, guided by this very mantra. We have set before us the goals of a Viksit Bharat and an Atmanirbhar Bharat.Our goal is to make India fully self-reliant as that is how a country can progress.Vijayadashami celebrates victory of good over evil.Government's priority is welfare of poor and deprived sections of society.Purpose of power is not to rule, but to ensure public welfare; this is the ideal of Lord Shri Ram.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Waterford: Three new arrests after couple and two children killed in arson attack
articles.summary: A man in his 50s and two women in their 30s were arrested by gardaí (Irish police) on Tuesday.
articles.body:
Gardaí (Irish police) have arrested three more people in connection with a suspected arson attack which killed four family members in Waterford.

A man in his 50s and two women in their 30s were arrested by gardaí on Tuesday. A man aged in his 20s and a woman in her 30s were previously charged in connection with the fatal attack.

Kim English, Philip English and two of their children - nine-year-old Jayden and 12-year-old Callum - died after their home in Birch Avenue, on the outskirts of Waterford was set on fire on Tuesday.

Two other children, who were also in the house at the time, remain in a critical condition in hospital in Crumlin.

Those arrested on Tuesday are currently being held in a station in the east of the Republic of Ireland.

articles.title: Italian banker was 'dropped to his death by mistake' when thugs dangled him out of his office window 'only to threaten'
articles.summary: David Rossi, the communications director of the Italian bank Monte dei Paschi di Siena, died in 2013.
articles.body: David Rossi, the communications director of the Italian bank Monte dei Paschi di Siena, died in 2013. It was believed till date that he committed suicide, as his body was found beneath an open window of the bank's headquarters in Siena. After 13 years, new evidence surfaced to a parliamentary commission that had been investigating the death and two unnamed men claimed that the ex-chairman of the bank sent thugs to threaten Rossi after Rossi decided to tell authorities about the bank's dealings with the mafia.But the plan was not to kill him, only to threaten him by dangling him from his office window. But then the grip slipped accidentally and Rossi dropped 60 ft to his death. The bank, at that time, was facing a corruption scandal and its finances were in shambles. The ex-chairman of the bank who ordered the threatening was Giuseppe Mussari.Reports claimed that Rossi was moving millions of euros from one account to another for the Grande Aracri clan, a powerful group within the southern Italian ’Ndrangheta organisation, and Rossi was going to tell the authorities about this.'I have done something stupid'A note was found in Rossi's bin which said: I have done something stupid and this was considered as a suicide note for years.One witness has now claimed that Mussari employed Gabriele Ceccherelli, a former member of a Florence team that plays calcio storico, a violent, medieval version of football, to orchestrate a plan to intimidate Mr Rossi, the Daily Mail reported. Ceccherelli sent two teammates to scare Rossi.Ceccherelli denied any involvement. "I know nothing about this; I don't know anyone involved in this case," he said. "The only time I've ever been to Siena was to buy a pair of shoes."Another witness said the hired thugs parked their van at the entrance to the alley to stop passers-by from spotting Rossi's body. CCTV footage also showed two men looking at the body on the street before walking away. Two initial inquiries concluded that he had taken his own life but his family insisted that he was murdered. The parliamentary inquiry was ordered in 2021.CCTV footage also raised suspicion as it showed him falling backwards from his office window, slamming into the ground on his back. He weakly moved his head and arms for around 20 minutes as he lay on the ground, before succumbing to his injuries.Mussari dismissed the allegations and said he would take legal action to clear his name.You use AI every day. articles.title: An Irish lottery winner took home £3.3 million in 2001; years later, a court heard how investments and a failed construction business left him struggling to repay a bank loan
articles.summary: In 2001, Cormac Handy collected lottery winnings worth £3.3 million, a sum that could have secured his financial future.
articles.body: In 2001, Cormac Handy collected lottery winnings worth £3.3 million, a sum that could have secured his financial future. More than a decade later, the Irishman was in Galway District Court over a bank loan he had guaranteed for someone else. Ulster Bank wanted him to repay €14,371, including the outstanding debt, costs and interest. Handy maintained that he could afford only €50 a month. By then, he had told the court, much of his fortune had disappeared through losses on investments and the collapse of a construction business he had entered with his brother. The hearing in March 2013 brought his earlier windfall into the discussion.Irish lottery winner Cormac Handy faced court over an unpaid bank loanHandy, who was originally from Clara, County Offaly, won £3,320,243 in 2001. By the time of the court proceedings, he was living in Rockbarton, Salthill, in Galway and working as a lecturer at Galway-Mayo Institute of Technology, now known as Atlantic Technological University.His appearance before the court was not about the lottery itself. Ulster Bank Ireland Ltd was seeking to enforce an earlier Circuit Court order requiring him to pay money owed under a loan for which he had acted as guarantor. The order had been made on August 30, 2012, and the bank wanted the repayments enforced.The amount in question was €14,371. That included €13,507 in debt, €624 in costs and expenses, and interest charged at 8 per cent a year. The bank sought monthly payments of €400, but Handy said his finances would not stretch that far.How investment losses eroded his lottery fortuneDuring the hearing reported on March 22, 2013, the court heard what had happened to a substantial portion of the money he had received more than a decade earlier. As reported by The Irish Times, Handy said he had lost €1.5 million through stocks and shares. He had also put money into a construction business with his brother, but that venture had collapsed.The account offered in court gave a partial explanation for how a multimillion-pound windfall had failed to leave him with enough readily available money to meet the bank's demand. Handy told the judge that he had paid off half his mortgage when he won and distributed some of the money among members of his family.His financial position had also become more difficult because of his housing costs. He said he had previously been paying €1,900 a month in interest-only mortgage payments. Those payments had since risen to €4,500 a month, covering the full mortgage repayment.Monthly bills came under scrutiny in lottery winner’s debt caseSean Acton, the solicitor representing Ulster Bank, examined the statement of means Handy had submitted ahead of the hearing. The document listed the household's regular expenses, including €650 a month for food, housekeeping and personal care. Heating costs came to €150, while car maintenance and repairs accounted for €120.The figures also included €42 for UPC broadband, €40 for Sky television, €90 for two mobile phones and €100 for clothing and footwear. Petrol for two cars cost €180 a month, with another €100 set aside for family occasions, birthdays, Christmas celebrations and meals out.Acton challenged Handy over the spending, suggesting that he was unwilling to repay the bank rather than genuinely unable to do so. Handy responded that the loan was not his own debt, although he acknowledged that he had stood as guarantor.By guaranteeing the loan, he had accepted responsibility for the debt if the original borrower failed to meet the required payments. The proceedings concerned the bank's attempt to recover the money under that arrangement.Why the judge questioned his mortgage and pension spendingJudge Mary Fahy also asked why Handy had not used more of his lottery winnings to clear his mortgage when he first received the money. She pointed out that he could have bought himself greater financial security by paying it off outright.Handy said he had repaid half the mortgage at the time and shared some of the winnings with his family. His explanation did not settle the question of how much money remained available to him by 2013, particularly given the investment losses, failed business and higher monthly housing costs he described. Another item in his statement of means drew the judge's attention. Handy was paying €165 a month into a private pension, despite holding a permanent, pensionable position at GMIT. Judge Fahy questioned whether that additional contribution should take priority over the money owed to the bank.Her remarks reflected the circumstances of the wider economic downturn, when households were being pressed to reduce spending. She argued that the pension payment was an expense Handy could reconsider while facing the repayment order. Reportedly, his solicitor, Antoinette McMahon, maintained that there was little money left after his existing commitments and repeated that he could manage only €50 a month.Court ordered repayments of €250 a monthJudge Fahy rejected the proposed €50 monthly payment. She considered it possible for Handy to pay more, taking account of the expenses he had declared and the private pension contribution. The judge ordered him to make installments of €250 a month, less than the €400 sought by the bank but five times the amount he had offered.In explaining her decision, Fahy remarked that Handy was still paying for things other people had been forced to give up during the difficult economic period. She also observed that he had a secure job with pension benefits. The judge described the order as a generous outcome for him and said he could appeal if he wished. The case did not establish that Handy had spent every euro of his lottery winnings, nor did it provide a complete accounting of his finances after 2001. More than 12 years after collecting £3.3 million, Handy was being ordered to repay a comparatively modest bank debt in monthly installments.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. In a statement, quoted by Reuters, it urged the US to "immediately correct wrong practices ... and revoke relevant discriminatory restrictions." articles.summary: At a rally in Kansas, US President Donald Trump highlighted recent unrest in France to warn against a Democratic victory in the upcoming midterm elections, framing the situation as a threat to American stability.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has invoked unrest in France to attack Democrats while campaigning for Republican Senator Roger Marshall in Kansas, where a closely contested race has emerged as Republicans face pressure ahead of the November midterm elections.Trump's Monday rally for Marshall focused on immigration, cultural issues and warnings about what he said could happen in the United States if Republicans lose ground.“I love you Kansas, but I'm here for a guy named Roger Marshall,” Trump told the crowd.During the rally, Trump referred to protests and violence in France, where demonstrations over living costs and underfunded public services have escalated into riots and looting in recent days. He used the unrest to frame the election as a choice between Republican leadership and what he portrayed as a threat posed by Democrats.“When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to do to America,” Trump said.Trump has repeatedly used the term “Dumocrats” to mock the opposition.The rally comes as Trump campaigns across Republican-leaning areas to help candidates defend their seats ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. Republicans are seeking to retain control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives amid voter concerns over the Iran war and rising prices.Kansas has long been a Republican stronghold. Trump won the state by 16% points in the 2024 presidential election, and a Democrat has not won a US Senate race there in 94 years. However, Marshall, who is seeking another term, is facing a close challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, a Methodist megachurch pastor.Hamilton has campaigned against Trump's tariff agenda and criticised what he describes as the president's “erratic leadership.”Trump attacked Hamilton during the rally, saying, “He wants you to repent for being born White.”Marshall, meanwhile, emphasised cultural issues, including opposition to what he called “radical Islam”. He described Hamilton as “too woke” for Kansas because he supported gay pride parades, drawing boos from the crowd.“We need someone who can sort heifers and steers,” Marshall said.Hamilton's campaign dismissed the rally's message, arguing that it did not address the economic concerns facing residents.“Nothing said at the rally can distract from the fact Kansans are being crushed by rising gas and diesel prices, struggling to access affordable healthcare, and are tired of Washington corruption,” campaign spokesperson Tyson Brody said.In a video released on Monday, Hamilton welcomed Trump to Kansas and said Trump supporters had a place in his campaign. He said he would work with the president where their interests aligned, while opposing federal policies that harmed farmers and rural hospitals.The contest in Kansas reflects wider challenges facing Republicans as they seek to hold their congressional majorities in November. Trump has been campaigning across areas that he won comfortably in previous elections as part of a 32-day campaign blitz.​You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Trump ‘frustrated and angry’ says Rubio; rejects reports of shift in Ukraine policy
articles.summary: US secretary of state Marco Rubio on Tuesday said Washington had not changed its policy on weapons assistance and intelligence sharing with Ukraine, while
articles.body: US secretary of state Marco Rubio on Tuesday said Washington had not changed its policy on weapons assistance and intelligence sharing with Ukraine, while asserting that President Donald Trump was “frustrated and angry” over the lack of progress in negotiations to end the war.Rubio, who arrived in Mumbai on Tuesday at the start of a three-day visit to India, said the US wanted to end the conflict amid mounting casualties and the risk of it spreading to other regions, PTI reported.“The President made it very clear, and there are no such changes. So none of that has changed. And I see reporting that it has, which is not accurate,” Rubio told reporters, rejecting reports of a shift in US support for Kyiv.Rubio said the US president was “most certainly angry and frustrated at the lack of progress in those negotiations”.Ukraine has been facing shortages of US-made Patriot air defence systems and PAC-3 interceptors, which can intercept Russian ballistic missiles. Intensified Russian attacks over the past two months have forcedUkrainians to increasingly seek shelter, with air raid alerts becoming part of daily life.Addressing concerns over the availability of missile interceptors, Rubio said several countries had requested them from Washington, describing them as the “most in-demand product” in the defence sector.“When a country doesn't get interceptors from the United States, it's not because we're denying. We have our own. We have minimum standards that we have to meet internally in our base presence all over the world,” he said.“We have a global defence footprint, and many of our installations around the world are part of defence, air defence. So there's nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine,” Rubio added.Rubio also rejected allegations that Washington had withheld intelligence that could have helped Ukraine anticipate Russian strikes on October 13 and 18. He said the failure to detect the attacks was not due to a lack of information provided by the US.“That is not because America did not provide information. I saw somebody associated with the Ukrainian government say that people in Ukraine are dying because the US is denying them information. That's scandalous. That's outrageous; that's simply not true. That's not accurate,” he said.On Monday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv had again received no early warning of the attacks from partner countries that had previously shared intelligence.Rubio said the problem could have been related to Ukraine's ability to process and act on the information it received. “That's possible. We are looking at it,” he said.“Our understanding is that, to the extent that happened on the 13th and on the 18th (October), it was a technical matter. It was not the result of any sort of US directive not to provide advance warning of a strike,” Rubio said.“We are providing the same warnings to them now that we always have,” he added.You use AI every day. articles.title: A 30-room home where Australian painter Frederick McCubbin lived is at the centre of an ownership fight after a caretaker spent 22 years there
articles.summary: A historic 30-room house where Australian painter Frederick McCubbin created some of his best-known works is at the centre of a legal dispute over its
articles.body: A historic 30-room house where Australian painter Frederick McCubbin created some of his best-known works is at the centre of a legal dispute over its ownership. It is known as Fontainebleau; the property stands in Mount Macedon in regional Victoria and was the only home McCubbin owned in the early 1900s.The two-storey house is now in a neglected condition. The dispute involves its five joint proprietors and Trevor Hoare, a caretaker who has lived there for 22 years. According to the ABC News, the Supreme Court of Victoria has heard the dispute, while Hoare’s ownership application remains under assessment by Land Use Victoria.How did McCubbin’s former 30-room home become part of a legal disputeFontainebleau is a sprawling, two-storey timber and fibro residence in Mount Macedon, about an hour’s drive north of Melbourne. Frederick McCubbin, one of Australia’s best-known impressionist painters, stayed there during weekends and holidays while continuing his teaching role at the National Gallery of Victoria School in Melbourne.The house is where he painted works including ‘The Pioneer’, alongside other paintings inspired by the surrounding area. The property has been listed on the Victorian Heritage Register since 2010 for its historical and architectural significance to the state. However, its present condition has become a concern. The Supreme Court of Victoria heard claims that the residence had black mould, evidence of vermin, and wheelie bins collecting rainwater. The property is owned by five joint proprietors, including brothers Paul and Mark Cutler.Caretaker seeks ownership after spending 22 years at the propertyTrevor Hoare has lived at Fontainebleau under an agreement with Mark Cutler made in March 2004. He applied for adverse possession in November 2025, withdrew that application and submitted another in February 2026. Adverse possession allows a person to claim ownership of land after at least 15 years of uninterrupted, exclusive and unauthorised possession.Hoare’s lawyer, Kieran Hickey, told the court that his client was an elderly pensioner who had put time, labour and money into maintaining the residence. Hickey said, "Mr Hoare regards it as his home. He has adult children who attend regularly, he has not lived anywhere else except for family and health reasons including last winter”."He doesn't own any other property."Caretaker and owner clash over locks at McCubbin’s former homeThe legal dispute intensified after the locks at Fontainebleau were changed in March at Paul Cutler’s direction. This happened a few weeks after Hoare had first put locks on the property. Cutler’s lawyer, Timothy Sowden, told the court that his client had messaged Hoare in February after learning about the adverse possession claim and withdrawn permission for the caretaker to remain at the residence.The lawyer said, "It was a tit for tat arrangement." Associate Justice Ian Irving ordered Cutler to provide Hoare with possession of the property and hand over all keys by 4 pm on 8 April. The order also requires Hoare to allow Heritage Victoria to inspect the residence and carry out any urgent repairs.Why are heritage officials concerned about the condition of FontainebleauFontainebleau’s historic significance has made its condition another important issue in the dispute. Heritage Victoria had required the owners to engage a heritage consultant to inspect the property and prepare a schedule of works by February 2026. An extension was granted because of the legal proceedings. Sowden told the court that the residence needed to be made “safe to walk through” and estimated that a biohazard clean would cost $60,000.Hoare’s lawyer said his client did not stand in the way of Heritage Victoria addressing the property and had himself lodged a heritage claim. The house has a history beyond McCubbin’s time there. His family continued living at Fontainebleau after he died in 1917, and historical records show that the property was later used as a guest house before becoming a private residence. The court case was scheduled to return in August in 2026.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Christina Applegate says she was wrongfully diagnosed with MS
articles.summary: She said in a Tuesday release of her Messy podcast that she was not happy about the new information and her symptoms have only "gotten worse".
articles.body:
Christina Applegate thought she was living with multiple sclerosis (MS) for five years, until recently discovering she had been given a wrong diagnosis.

The actress, known for hits like Anchorman and Married With Children, said she was "not happy at all" about the news and in tears when she found out.

"You don't get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I'm better," Applegate said in an episode of her Messy podcast released on Tuesday. "If anything, I've gotten worse."

The two-part episode, co-hosted by Jamie Sigler, ends a recent break she took to process the information. An investigation into what is causing her debilitating symptoms - which she experiences daily - will begin next week.

"I'm back at square one where I don't know what's going on with me," she said.

In the podcast, Applegate said that "all of a sudden, a few years ago", her doctor suggested ending her infusion treatment for MS to see how her body reacted.

During the time off, her body did not respond in a way that would indicate she had MS.

Doctors then looked into her case further and concluded she in fact did not have the autoimmune disease, which can cause muscle stiffness and problems with walking and talking.

"She came into my room and said, 'Congratulations, you don't have MS,' " Applegate said, recalling the moment.

"I was, like, not happy at all," she continued. "Everybody else was so happy."

Dr Marwa Kaisey, a guest on Tuesday's episode, said MS misdiagnoses are not uncommon because symptoms are inconsistent and there is no universal testing. One in five people people who were told they had MS "didn't actually have it".

"It's not like we have something like a pregnancy test that says 'yes, you have it. No, you don't,'" Kaisey said. "It's a list of criteria."

Applegate was first diagnosed with MS in August 2021, after experiencing symptoms for a while, saying at the time: "It's been a tough road. But as we all know, the road keeps on going."

Years later, she described being in a " real depression " and said in a 2024 episode of her podcast that "I don't enjoy living. I don't enjoy it. I don't enjoy things anymore".

She had said in a New York Times interview that she could not walk without a cane and used a wheelchair during filming of the Netflix series Dead To Me.
