articles.title: 'Enough drama in the ‌world': Prince Harry says he wants to reconcile with family after years of rift
articles.summary: Prince Harry hinted at a potential reconciliation with his family after years of rift.
articles.body: Prince Harry hinted at a potential reconciliation with his family after years of rift. He said he wants to repair his strained relationships with his father, King Charles III, and older brother, Prince William, urging his family to move on from past differences."With everything else that's going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile," Harry told GQ magazine in an interview published Tuesday.The Duke of Sussex, 42, acknowledged that his family's rift had attracted public attention because it reflected struggles many people experience in their own lives, including disagreements between siblings and strained relationships between parents and children. "Some people don't want it to work out. I want it to work out.""Sibling disagreements, broken relationships between kids and their parents, kids and one parent - that continues to come up with me the whole time with people that I speak to," he added on public finding it "relatable"The prince also acknowledged that repairing relationships does not mean erasing past hurt. "For me, there's enough drama in the world and enough drama in people's lives than to continue with issues with family," he said. "It's not worth it."He added that while "scars stick around forever", he wanted to encourage people to let go of the past and work towards reconciliation.Harry also spoke about his family's return to Britain, saying that enrolling his children in a British school had been particularly meaningful to him."I didn't know how important it was to me. I always thought it was going to be something that we would try and do, but now they've been in school for two weeks. They're loving it and it's just giving them a whole different experience," he told GQ.He also expressed hope that his troubled relationship with the British press could improve, saying he wanted to draw a line under past disputes. "My hope is that it will change," he said, adding that he hoped all sides could leave aspects of the past behind and work towards the greater good.He also talked about carrying the grief of losing his mother at a young age. "I love the fact that I'm able to now sort of carry the memory of my mother with me, with my work, rather than it hold me down, pull me back, or wallowing in that grief," he said. However, he added, "I certainly don't want any sympathy. That's where we're way past that. Why? Because I'm a prince. I've got a support network around me, I've done different forms of therapy, and I put in the work. I wonder where I would be if I didn't - it could be a very different situation."The royal riftHarry and his wife, Meghan, stepped back from their roles as working royals in 2020 and moved to California. Their departure was followed by public criticism of the royal institution, a series of revelations about family tensions and Harry's memoir, Spare, which detailed his strained relationship with William.Harry has also pursued legal action against British newspaper groups over alleged unlawful information gathering, further intensifying his long-running conflict with parts of the press.Although Harry has met his father in recent months after the latter's cancer diagnosis, he has not made such contact with his brother.You use AI every day. articles.title: K3G lessons, cricket, no spice: How is Prince William preparing to come to India
articles.summary: Britain’s Prince William's preparations for his Mumbai visit have taken a distinctly Indian turn.
articles.body: Britain’s Prince William's preparations for his Mumbai visit have taken a distinctly Indian turn. The Prince of Wales has spoken about his fascination with India's love for cricket, his meeting with filmmaker Karan Johar and his excitement about bringing the Earthshot Prize to the city.He said he is looking forward to returning to Mumbai for the 2026 Earthshot Prize, drawn by the city’s energy.In an interview with the BBC, William spoke about meeting Bollywood filmmaker Karan Johar, who has been helping the prize establish itself in India. He also promised to watch one of his films after being introduced to the classic Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham.William said he was excited about bringing the Earthshot Prize to Mumbai, where the winners of the 2026 edition will be announced on November 17 during a televised awards ceremony. The prize, which supports projects addressing environmental challenges, will be held in India for what organisers describe as its biggest edition yet.William on meeting Karan JoharWilliam spoke warmly about meeting filmmaker Karan Johar, who has been helping the Earthshot Prize connect with audiences in India.“Really cool. I mean, he's, again, an icon and he's been so helpful in kind of being able to help the Earthshot Prize land well in India. We want to make it a truly Indian Earthshot Prize. It's the biggest one we've done,” he said.Asked whether Johar had introduced him to any of his Bollywood films, William said the filmmaker had been modest about his work.“No, he's been very modest, but I'm sure as time goes on, he'll introduce some more films to me,” he said.The interviewer then suggested that William watch Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham, the 2001 family drama directed by Johar and popularly known as K3G.“K3G might be easier,” William said, agreeing that the abbreviated title would be easier to remember.“If you meet Karan again, tell him, I'm going to watch your film K3G,” the interviewer told him.“Okay, got it. I'll mention that to him when I see him,” William replied.William on his Mumbai visitIn the BBC interview, Prince William offers a spicy confession ahead of his India visit, “My spicy intake is pretty limited. I start sweating. It's terrible.”The interviewer is quick to remind him that he will need to get used to it, saying, “You need to get a hold on that because you're going to Mumbai for the Earthshot prize.”Speaking about Mumbai, William said, “So I'm really looking forward to the vibe. It's one of the most vibrant cities I've ever been to. The love of cricket out there is phenomenal. I've never known anything like it. And I love my sports. Obviously, football is my number one. But seeing how the Indians love their cricket, this felt like a really fun thing to do to get some of the icons from cricket on the mall in an iconic situation and just kind of get everyone excited about the idea of Earthshot coming to Mumbai.”The prince was also asked about an unusual cricket match played at a shopping mall as part of the build-up to the event.“You've shut down the mall and you played a cricket match here. I mean, first time ever?” the interviewer asked.“First time ever. I think that's happened. Yes. I mean, rugby would be harder. So quite relieved we started with cricket,” William replied.What is the Earthshot Prize?Founded by William in 2020, the Earthshot Prize aims to accelerate environmental innovation and support solutions to climate change, pollution, habitat loss and other threats to the planet. Inspired by former US President John F Kennedy's 1962 Moonshot speech, the initiative aims to help “repair the planet” by 2030.The 2026 finalists include the Yellowstone to Yukon Conservation Initiative, which works with Indigenous communities, ranchers and governments to protect wildlife corridors across the Rocky Mountains, from Wyoming in the United States to north-western Canada.The initiative supports the creation of protected areas and wildlife crossings, including overpasses, underpasses and fencing that help animals cross busy roads safely. It is among 15 finalists competing across the prize's five categories.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 1996, an Oxfordshire man packed away his father's old cameras in a loft; nearly 30 years later, he uncovered a rare Victorian model that sold for £18,000, with proceeds pledged to wildlife conservation
articles.summary: A forgotten box of photography equipment stored in an Oxfordshire loft for nearly 30 years has revealed a very rare Victorian camera that sold at auction
articles.body: A forgotten box of photography equipment stored in an Oxfordshire loft for nearly 30 years has revealed a very rare Victorian camera that sold at auction for £18,000. The collection was first put away in 1996 by a homeowner who had inherited his father's belongings. Nearly 30 years later, during a routine house clearance, he found a late 19th-century folding camera made of mahogany and brass. It was tucked inside a leather case. According to cataloguing details and sales records released by Churchill Auctions, the historic camera attracted strong competition from international collectors before selling for a hammer price of £18,000. After the sale, the seller announced that a large part of the auction proceeds would go directly to UK wildlife conservation charities. The donation is in memory of his late father, who loved nature and was a keen amateur photographer.Decades of storage in a village homeThe camera equipment was first stored away in 1996, when the owner moved into his family home in Oxfordshire. The wooden crate was left untouched in an insulated loft for almost 30 years, surrounded by personal belongings, old books, and household items. When the homeowner decided to clear the attic, he brought several dusty cases downstairs to check what was inside. In one padded leather case, he found a well-preserved Victorian tailboard camera. It had brass fittings, its original bellows, and a carefully made optical lens dating from the late 1800s. According to a background account published by Churchill Auctions, the owner's father had bought the camera decades earlier at a local estate sale. However, the family had no idea of its historical importance or market value. The loft's dry and stable conditions helped protect the camera over the years. They prevented fungus from damaging the glass lenses and helped keep the polished mahogany woodwork from bending or changing shape.Expert evaluation and historical significanceRealising that the camera was an unusually fine example of early British photography equipment, the owner took it to Churchill Auctions for a professional valuation and assessment. Auctioneers and photography specialists at Churchill Auctions identified it as an outstanding late Victorian wet-plate or dry-plate camera. It was made during the period when British manufacturers were known for producing cameras from brass and mahogany. Specialists noted that many surviving cameras from the 1880s and 1890s show heavy wear, have missing parts, or have damaged leather bellows. In contrast, the camera found in the Oxfordshire loft was in almost museum-quality condition, with all its original brass fittings still in place. According to valuation notes from Churchill Auctions, well-preserved 19th-century cameras made by famous London manufacturers are becoming increasingly popular with private collectors, photography historians, and museum curators around the world.Auction room competition and sale resultsThe Victorian camera was listed as a major item in a recent fine art and antiques auction held by Churchill Auctions. Interest before the sale grew quickly as international buyers signed up to bid by phone and online. On auction day, strong competition pushed the price well above the initial estimates. The bidding eventually ended at £18,000. Auctioneers at Churchill Auctions confirmed that the winning bid came from a private collector who specialises in 19th-century scientific instruments and early optical equipment. The unexpected money gave the seller a chance to honour his father's lifelong interests.Funding wildlife conservation initiativesAfter the auction ended, the seller confirmed that the proceeds from the £18,000 sale would be donated to support local and national wildlife conservation funds. According to details shared by Churchill Auctions, the seller's father was a dedicated naturalist who spent decades recording the plants and animals found in the British countryside. By giving the money to wildlife protection groups, the family hopes to create a lasting legacy for nature linked to the long-forgotten camera. The donations will support local projects to restore natural habitats, manage woodlands, and protect native species across the region. In this way, a forgotten piece of Victorian history will help support modern efforts to protect wildlife and the natural environment.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2005, a Danish man moved into an ordinary suburban house and started building a garden wall the following year; two decades later it has castle towers, a four-metre moat and hundreds of visitors
articles.summary: On a quiet residential street near Aalborg, Denmark, one house looks as though it has wandered out of another century.
articles.body: On a quiet residential street near Aalborg, Denmark, one house looks as though it has wandered out of another century. There are towers where neighbours have garages, battlements where most homes have rooflines and a moat surrounding what was once an entirely ordinary suburban property. For Peter Hvid, what began as a garden wall has evolved over two decades into Casa Del Renaissance, a homemade medieval fantasy complete with a courtyard, drawbridge and towering stonework.From garden wall to castleAccording to an online report by Love Property, Hvid moved into the 1959-built detached house in 2005. A year later, after securing the necessary planning permission, he began building a wall around the garden. His childhood fascination with knights and castles provided the inspiration, while an interest in building gradually turned a simple boundary wall into something far more ambitious.The first tower appeared when Hvid wanted a sheltered outdoor space where people could sit in the shade. Another tower followed, then another. What started as a series of additions eventually became a complete architectural transformation, adds the report.If we go by the report, Hvid carried out roughly 90 per cent of the construction himself, despite having no formal trade or building qualification. Plumbing and electrical work required professionals, but much of the masonry, carpentry and decorative work became his own responsibility.A moat that kept growingThe scale of the project changed dramatically over the years. Hvid's original moat was only one metre wide and 10 metres long. Today, the water-filled trench is around four metres wide and extends around much of the property.Inside, the suburban house has been reshaped to create the atmosphere of a Renaissance fortress. The original 220-square-metre home has been reduced to about 180 square metres in places, largely because Hvid removed sections of the upper floor to create soaring six-metre-high ceilings, adds the report.The result includes a grand hall, a statement staircase, heavy wooden doors with iron fittings, a large candelabra and richly detailed wood panelling. A six-and-a-half-metre dining table in the knights' hall was built by Hvid after he failed to find one large enough to match his vision.Medieval details meet modern lifeThe Love Property report also states that despite the medieval appearance, Casa Del Renaissance remains a thoroughly modern home. Central heating, electricity and a contemporary bathroom provide the conveniences expected of a 21st-century residence, while fireplaces, armour, heraldic motifs and traditional materials create the illusion of stepping several centuries into the past.Hvid is particularly interested in traditional craftsmanship and has incorporated salvaged and repurposed materials wherever possible. Even small details, including traditionally forged iron nails, have become part of the home's carefully constructed character, explains the report from August 2026.The project has never followed a fixed blueprint. New coats of arms, fittings and architectural details continue to appear as Hvid discovers materials or develops new ideas, the report also explains.From local curiosity to attractionIn its early years, the unusual construction attracted plenty of attention in Gistrup. What may once have seemed like an eccentric suburban experiment has since become a local landmark, drawing visitors from beyond the town.As per the report, Hvid opens the property to the public once a year for an open castle event. The most recent gathering attracted around 600 visitors, while demand for tours has at times been so high that he has had to temporarily limit access.The property also hosts an annual Halloween event for local children. What began as a one-person production has grown into an elaborate community occasion involving 16 actors, with local businesses helping provide sweets and treats, informs the online report.A castle that may never be finishedAfter nearly 20 years of construction, Casa Del Renaissance remains a work in progress. Hvid has repeatedly reached the point where he believes the latest tower or addition will be the final one, only to imagine another improvement.The latest idea includes a royal guard, with friends already acquiring matching uniforms and helmets for appearances during feasts and public events.For Hvid, the appeal is ultimately less about creating a perfect historical replica than building a private fairytale world. After working as a caseworker, he returns home to a place where medieval feasts, knights and castle towers replace the routines of ordinary suburbia. And with his partner Maria considering the property her future summer palace, Casa Del Renaissance may yet gain its queen.Images Courtesy: Love PropertyYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: No double standards on terror, need unified action to dismantle its entire ecosystem: Rajnath at SCO
articles.summary: Defence minister Rajnath Singh, in the presence of Pakistan’s deputy PM and foreign minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar at a Shanghai Cooperation Organisation
articles.body: Defence minister Rajnath Singh, in the presence of Pakistan’s deputy PM and foreign minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar at a Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) meeting in Dushanbe, said on Tuesday that there should not be “double standards” on terrorism as it “not only harms innocent lives but also investment and commerce”.Addressing the 25th meeting of the council of heads of govt (CHG) of SCO, Rajnath called upon member states to make concerted efforts to dismantle the entire ecosystem of terrorism, describing the menace as one of the gravest threats to peace and development. “Terrorism results in the loss of innocent lives and disrupts investment and commerce. It radicalises societies and deprives youth of the opportunities they rightfully deserve. There can be no justification for terrorism, no double standards in addressing it, and no place for those who finance, support, or provide safe havens to terrorists,” he said.Hinting at the supply chain disruptions due to the West Asia conflict, Rajnath, who represents India on behalf of PM Narendra Modi, said, “In the changing global economic environment, SCO countries will have to work together on resilient supply chains, better trade and investment, and technology-driven development. India's vision is clear—ensuring inclusive development for all member countries through security, connectivity, and opportunity.”Pointing out that India supports initiatives that link markets, facilitate trade and create new avenues for development, the minister said that initiatives such as the International North-South Transport Corridor and the Chabahar Port can contribute significantly to connecting Central Asia with broader markets. Stressing that the benefits of economic cooperation must reach all sections of society, he reaffirmed India’s support for the adoption of an action plan for the multilateral trade and economic cooperation programme for the period 2026-2030.The minister stressed that connectivity must be based on consultation and respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all countries, adding that projects not founded on these principles will not be sustainable. He emphasised the need to move beyond physical connectivity by simplifying customs procedures, promoting digital documentation, improving logistics and adopting interoperable digital solutions to reduce the cost of doing business across the region. He urged the SCO to build on the strong foundation established over the past 25 years and chart a forward-looking roadmap focused on consensus-driven cooperation and tangible outcomes.Rajnath recalled the deliberations at the SCO Summit in Bishkek in Aug-Sept, when PM Modi underlined the need for concrete steps by the organisation on issues related to security, connectivity, and opportunity. “India believes that the SCO must remain efficient and steadfast in its adherence to the principles of sovereign equality, consensus, and mutual respect. A greater number of institutions does not necessarily translate into greater achievements. New mechanisms should focus on clearly identified needs, avoid duplication, and prioritise delivering practical value to Member States,” he said.Later at a meeting with the Indian diaspora in Dushanbe, the minister said, “Guided by the philosophy of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, India aspires to become a nation that combines prosperity, knowledge and strength with a commitment to global peace and the well-being of humanity”. articles.title: Farm loan waiver delay deepens drought distress in Marathwada
articles.summary: Marathwada drought worsens as Maharashtra farm loan waiver OTS beneficiary lists are delayed, leaving farmers uncertain; Nanded suicide raises concerns.
articles.body: Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar: As drought tightens its grip on Marathwada, uncertainty over Maharashtra’s farm loan waiver scheme and delays in releasing beneficiary lists under its One Time Settlement (OTS) component are adding to farmers’ distress, with the alleged suicide of a Nanded farmer bringing the issue into sharp focus.Farmer Shankar Kshirsagar of Borgaon Telang village in Nanded district, who had an outstanding crop loan of Rs 2.08 lakh, allegedly died by suicide in his field after repeatedly failing to find his name in the loan waiver beneficiary lists. Before his death, he recorded a video claiming that despite repeated announcements of loan relief, he had received no benefit.The case has triggered fresh questions over the implementation of the Punyashlok Ahilyadevi Holkar Shetkari Karj Mukti Yojana 2026, under which crop loans of up to Rs 2 lakh are to be waived.The problem is most acute for farmers covered under the OTS component. Under the scheme, farmers whose outstanding dues exceeded Rs 2 lakh as of March 31, 2026, must first clear the amount above Rs 2 lakh before becoming eligible for the waiver. However, even months after the scheme was announced, many farmers say they still do not know whether they qualify.Deputy Registrar of Cooperative Societies, Nanded, K B Fiske acknowledged that the OTS rollout has yet to begin. “The names of eligible farmers are uploaded on the portal. However, the lists of beneficiaries are not yet released officially anywhere,” he said.Farmer rights activists say the delay is creating anxiety in villages already reeling from crop losses, debt and water scarcity. “The inordinate delay in releasing official lists of farmers eligible for the loan waiver scheme may push many farmers to the brink,” said activist Jayaji Suryawanshi. “Forget Rs 2 lakh outstanding dues, even those farmers who have dues less than Rs 2 lakh are awaiting their names in the lists. State govt must take serious cognisance and address bottlenecks and red-tapism even at the level of banks,” he added.State govt had projected that around 56 lakh farmers would benefit from the scheme. However, the cooperation department has so far released only three lists covering about 24.7 lakh beneficiaries, less than half the projected figure.A senior revenue department official said govt may first complete the process for farmers with crop loans below Rs 2 lakh before rolling out the OTS component. “The OTS scheme for loans above Rs 2 lakh is scheduled to be rolled out sequentially after the first phases. There is, however, no official communication,” the official said on condition of anonymity.Opposition parties have alleged that the exercise has been slowed by efforts to verify central tax records and filter out ineligible beneficiaries.Stay updated with the latest Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar news. articles.title: Indian-origin lab owner charged in US over $66.2 million bogus Covid test claims: DOJ
articles.summary: Rajesh Patel, an Indian-origin lab co-owner, faces charges for submitting $66.2 million in fraudulent COVID-19 test claims, allegedly fabricating results for non-existent patients.
articles.body: An Indian-origin man in the US has been charged with allegedly submitting $66.2 million in bogus claims for COVID-19 tests that were never conducted, US Department of Justice said.Rajesh “Raj” Patel, 52, of Schaumburg, Illinois, faces five counts of wire fraud over an alleged scheme involving at least 380,000 polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests between May 2021 and April 2022. Prosecutors allege that Patel generated fake negative test results and used them to claim payments from a federal programme for uninsured people.Patel was co-owner and chief operating officer of a clinical laboratory in Hillside, Illinois, that processed PCR tests during the pandemic. According to court documents, the laboratory agreed with Meridian Medical Staffing Inc. in March 2021, paying the company tens of millions of dollars to collect samples and provide biological information about purported patients.Investigators allege many of these patients either did not exist or had never provided samples to Meridian. Despite this, Patel created negative results for at least 380,000 tests that the laboratory had not performed.The laboratory used those results to bill the US Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) Uninsured Program, which covered COVID-19 testing for people without health insurance during the pandemic. It submitted about $66.2 million in claims and received approximately $44.1 million in payments, prosecutors said. Patel obtained around $28 million from the scheme.Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s Fraud Division said Patel allegedly exploited the public health emergency for personal gain by fabricating test results and billing the government.If convicted, Patel faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison on each of the five wire fraud counts.The Justice Department said its Health Care Fraud Strike Force Programme has charged more than 6,200 defendants since 2007 in cases involving more than $45 billion in alleged fraudulent billing to federal healthcare programmes and private insurers.You use AI every day.
